title: Data Analysis with Spreadsheets
summary: Use formulas, clean data, calculate summary statistics, build pivot tables and lookups, make clear charts and follow a responsible analysis process.
audience: Students, office workers, business owners and aspiring analysts

lessons.title: Spreadsheet basics: cells, formulas and functions

body.p: A spreadsheet is a grid of rows and columns. Each box is a cell with an address such as B3, meaning column B, row 3. Cells hold text, numbers or formulas. A formula always begins with an equals sign and updates automatically when the data changes.

list: =SUM(B2:B10) adds a range of numbers.
=AVERAGE(B2:B10) finds the mean.
=MIN and =MAX find the smallest and largest values.
=COUNT counts cells that contain numbers.
=IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail") returns a result based on a test.

body.p: Use absolute references with dollar signs, such as $B$1, to stop a reference changing when you copy a formula. A relative reference such as B1 shifts when copied down a column. Example: if prices are in column B and a tax rate is in $E$1, then =B2*$E$1 can be copied down safely.

body.tip: Keep one fact per cell, one record per row and a header for each column. Tidy data is easy to analyse.

body.p: Real data is messy. Names have extra spaces, dates use different formats, and numbers are stored as text. Analysts often spend most of their time cleaning data before they can learn anything from it.

list: Duplicates: the same record entered twice.
Missing values: blank cells that need a rule, such as leave blank or fill with a default.
Inconsistent spelling: Lagos, lagos and LAGOS counted as different places.
Wrong types: numbers stored as text, so they do not add up.
Outliers: values far from the rest, which may be errors or real cases.

body.p: Useful tools include sorting, filtering, remove duplicates, find and replace, TRIM for extra spaces and text-to-columns. Always keep a copy of the original data and record what you changed, so the work can be checked.

body.tip: Never overwrite the raw data. Work on a copy.

body.p: Summary statistics describe a data set in a few numbers. The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most frequent value. The range is the largest minus the smallest.

Example: scores 40, 50, 50, 60, 100. The mean is 300 ÷ 5 = 60. The median is 50. The mode is 50. The range is 100 - 40 = 60. The single high score pulls the mean above the median, so the median is a better description of a typical score here.

list: Standard deviation shows how far values typically lie from the mean; a small one means values are close together.
Percentage change = (new - old) ÷ old × 100. From 80 to 100 is (100 - 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%.
Percentage of total = part ÷ total × 100.

body.tip: Always look at the shape of the data and at outliers, not only the mean.

body.p: A pivot table summarises a large table quickly. You drag fields into rows, columns and values, and the sheet calculates totals, counts or averages for each group. For sales data, you could see total sales by region and month in seconds.

A lookup finds a value in a table using a key. XLOOKUP and VLOOKUP return, for example, the price of a product from its code. The key must match exactly, so clean your data first. Use IFERROR to show a friendly message when no match is found.

list: Use SUMIF or SUMIFS to add values that meet a condition.
Use COUNTIF to count how many times something appears.
Refresh a pivot table after changing the source data.

body.tip: Give your data table a clear name and keep it free of blank rows so pivots read all the data.

body.p: A chart should make one point clearly. Choose the right type. Use a line chart for change over time, a bar chart to compare categories, a scatter plot to see relationships between two numbers, and a pie chart only for a few parts of a whole.

list: Give the chart a title that states the message, such as 'Sales fell in March'.
Label axes and include units.
Start bar charts at zero. A truncated axis exaggerates differences.
Use few colours and keep text readable on phones.
Remove clutter such as heavy gridlines.

body.p: A dashboard combines a few key charts and numbers on one page for decision-makers. Show the most important numbers first and update them regularly.
Before sharing a chart, ask a colleague what message they take from it. If they miss the point, simplify the design until the message is obvious at a glance.

lessons.title: The analysis process and responsible use of data

body.p: Good analysis follows a process. Start with a clear question. Collect data. Clean it. Explore and summarise. Test ideas. Present findings and recommend actions. Always check that the data can actually answer the question.

list: Correlation is not causation: ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other.
Small samples can mislead.
Averages can hide differences between groups.
Cherry-picking: showing only the data that supports your view.

body.p: Protect personal data. Remove names and ID numbers when sharing, follow your organisation's rules and data protection law, and be honest about uncertainty. Explain your method so others can repeat it.

body.tip: End every analysis with: what does this mean, and what should we do next?
